item.title: China pledges greater fiscal support in H2
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
China pledges greater fiscal support in H2 New measures in the pipeline to help spur domestic demand, stabilize investment China will accelerate fiscal spending and roll out fresh measures to strengthen fiscal-financial coordination in the second half of the year — moves that are expected to help shore up domestic demand, stabilize investment and put the broader economy on a firmer footing, officials and experts said. The planned upgrade in fiscal support follows a mixed performance in July, with new growth drivers maintaining strong momentum even as key consumption and investment indicators came under pressure — a weakness experts attributed in part to slower fiscal spending. With ample maneuvering room, faster bond issuances and quick rollout of new policy-based financial instruments, experts said a more expansionary fiscal stance in the second half should keep the economy on track to meet its full-year growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent. "We will speed up fiscal spending at an appropriate pace in the second half and improve the efficiency of funds use," Liao Min, vice-minister of finance, said at a news conference on Friday. The pledge came as China's general public budget expenditure reached 16.29 trillion yuan ($2.4 trillion) in the first seven months, up 1.3 percent year-on-year, according to data from the Ministry of Finance. General public budget revenue increased 5.8 percent to 14.37 trillion yuan during the same period. Boosting domestic demand will remain a key focus. By the end of July, local governments had issued 2.4 trillion yuan in new special-purpose bonds, Liao said, with more than 2 trillion yuan worth of such bonds and ultra-long-term special treasury bonds to be issued in the second half. Song Yu, chief China economist at UBS Securities, said that as fiscal spending and bond issuance gather pace, government consumption should recover from its second-quarter slowdown and government investment is also likely to pick up. Vice-Minister Liao said China has also refined a six-policy fiscal-financial coordination package backed by 100 billion yuan in central government funding, with the latest changes taking effect on Aug 1. Introduced earlier this year, the package combines loan interest subsidies, financing guarantees and risk compensation to better leverage public funds, spur consumption and drive private investment. Under the package, newly issued working capital loans for micro, small and medium-sized private enterprises and all new credit card installment transactions are eligible for interest subsidies. The number of participating financial institutions in the two business loan subsidy programs increased to about 400 from about 100, while maximum subsidized loan amounts for businesses and subsidy caps for consumers were also raised. "The measures send a clear signal that policymakers are seeking to shore up confidence among private investors, encourage investment by micro, small and medium-sized enterprises and boost household consumption," said Shi Yinghua, director of the Chinese Academy of Fiscal Sciences' Research Center for Macroeconomics. Li Xuhong, vice-president and professor at the Beijing National Accounting Institute, said the broader subsidy coverage could magnify the impact of a relatively modest fiscal outlay by leveraging more bank lending, helping to spur consumer spending. In the seven months since its rollout, the package has benefited residents on about 113 million occasions and supported around 6.22 million enterprises, the ministry said. Further measures are in the pipeline. "We are working on additional fiscal-financial coordination measures, which will be rolled out in the second half," Vice-Minister Liao said. Su Jian, director of Peking University's National Center for Economic Research, said the next step should be "to shift from subsidizing interest payments to bolstering household incomes". Direct transfers to households in categories such as childcare, pensions and medical insurance would provide a more fundamental boost for consumption, he said. China is also pressing ahead with its consumer goods trade-in program, allocating 187.5 billion yuan so far this year and helping generate about 1.32 trillion yuan in related sales. Luo Zhiheng, chief economist and head of the research institute at Yuekai Securities, suggested further refining the program, while broadening similar policies to cover services.

item.title: Pop Mart H1 performance upbeat
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
Pop Mart H1 performance upbeat Pop Mart International Group Ltd's business in China remained its biggest growth engine in the first half, with revenue in its home market climbing 47.3 percent even as the collectible toy maker warned that its breakneck expansion is likely to moderate after last year's Labubu-driven boom. The company's revenue in China rose to 12.2 billion yuan ($1.82 billion) in the six months ended June, while the company added just 10 net new stores, bringing its network to 455 outlets. The results suggest the company is generating more sales from existing stores and its expanding membership base rather than relying on rapid store openings. Registered members increased to 82.4 million from 72.6 million at the end of last year. Members accounted for 92.9 percent of sales during the period, while the repurchase rate reached 51.6 percent. Group revenue rose 23.8 percent to 17.17 billion yuan during the first half, while adjusted net profit increased to 5.16 billion yuan. Gross margin improved to 69.7 percent and adjusted net margin reached 30 percent, reflecting continued profitability despite slower growth than last year's record pace. The shares fell as much as 8 percent in early trading on Friday after the earnings release as investors focused on management's more cautious outlook. Founder and Chief Executive Wang Ning said the company may not achieve its previously announced target of 20 percent annual revenue growth, citing a much tougher comparison with the second half of last year when Labubu, Pop Mart's best-selling collectible character, became a global phenomenon. "Last year's third quarter set an exceptionally high base, so the pressure in the second half will be greater than in the first," Wang told analysts on the earnings call. "We will not adopt aggressive strategies simply to pursue growth." Instead, the company is prioritizing operational improvements after a year in which explosive demand exposed weaknesses across its supply chain, store operations and inventory management, he added. "Last year was a case where strong sales masked many underlying problems," Wang said. "Consumers were constantly facing sold-out products, long queues and rush buying. That shouldn't be the norm." Looking ahead, Wang announced a share repurchase program worth between 2 billion yuan and 5 billion yuan over the next six months. Globally, Pop Mart now operates 676 stores and 2,827 Robo Shops, adding 46 stores and 190 vending machines during the first half. The company has established operations in more than 20 countries and regions and employs more than 12,000 people worldwide. Overseas growth began to normalize after last year's surge, with performance diverging across regions. Revenue in the Asia-Pacific market fell 9.7 percent to 2.58 billion yuan in the first half, while revenue in the Americas declined 16.5 percent to 1.89 billion yuan. Europe and other markets bucked the trend, with revenue rising 5.9 percent to 505.7 million yuan. Co-Chief Operating Officer Si De said online sales overseas have slowed as traffic returned to more typical levels following last year's Labubu frenzy. While offline sales growth has also moderated, single store productivity and customer traffic remain healthy, he said. Rather than rolling out larger flagship stores broadly, Pop Mart plans to focus upgrades on key markets while maintaining its standard overseas store size of about 150 to 200 square meters.

item.title: Yarlung Zangbo River, Nyingchi, Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
Flowing through the mountains of Nyingchi in Xizang, the Yarlung Zangbo River has carved the Yarlung Zangbo Grand Canyon, widely regarded as the world's deepest and longest canyon. Here, the river forms a great bend beneath majestic Mount Namjagbarwa, creating a breathtaking landscape where snow-capped peaks, dramatic gorges, and lush forests come together in harmony. Shaped by the canyon's unique valley climate, the region is rich in biodiversity and a vibrant Tibetan cultural heritage. Whether you're admiring Mount Namjagbarwa, exploring the canyon's hidden wonders, or experiencing the remarkable meeting of the Tibetan Plateau and lush forests, you'll discover the awe-inspiring beauty of one of Xizang's most spectacular natural landscapes. www.chinabound.cn Travel with ease in China, and with meaning.

item.title: 'China Cool' tourism opens eyes and minds
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
'China Cool' tourism opens eyes and minds In the sizzling summer of 2026, when "China Cool" became a buzzword on social media feeds worldwide, China's tourism market was experiencing a hot streak of its own. As global temperatures soared, so did the number of foreigners coming to China to escape the summer heat. In the first half of 2026, the National Immigration Administration recorded 22.91 million entries by foreign nationals, up 20.4 percent year-on-year. Visa-free entries surged 30.6 percent to 17.8 million, accounting for 77.7 percent of the total arrivals. These figures suggest that China is emerging as a popular summer destination for globetrotters around the world. The reason for the surge is obvious. Summer is the peak holiday season, and China has vast expanses with a relatively cool climate. Visa-free policies provided just the push needed to make travelers choose China with their feet. There is also a psychological dimension to this unprecedented rise in summer tourism. Many of the foreign travelers who come to escape the heat want to go somewhere cool. But the temperature is just one aspect of what "cool" means. Traveling abroad brings many new experiences, but the uncertainty can also lead to stress. In this sense, China offers a travel environment with relatively little friction and a high degree of predictability. While the temperature at the destination may not be any different, the experience is more manageable. Visa-free entry, 240-hour visa-free transit, convenient payment options, convenience stores that stay open late, high-speed railway information screens and easily accessible border checkpoints are more than just infrastructural improvements. Together, they reduce the uncertainty that people often face in an unfamiliar setting. This might explain why the most viral moments often capture the mundane. Under the "China Cool" trend, videos of foreign visitors riding high-speed trains, traveling in subways, sleeping on bamboo mats, savoring wontons at night markets, practicing traditional exercises and watching basketball in village squares are taking center stage. These are new experiences for foreigners, but they don't make one feel less independent simply because they are unfamiliar. Instead, they offer a rare opportunity to step into the rhythm of everyday life and, for a few days, live like a local. It is a deeper form of cultural travel. Perhaps the essence of "China Cool" lies in the erosion of stereotypes. When we lack knowledge about a group or place, we often rely on simplified assumptions, which then shape our judgments about almost everyone in the group. In this sense, stereotypes are mental shortcuts that help us make decisions when information is limited. But they come at a cost. They can distort reality and allow hearsay to overshadow first-hand experience. For places we have never visited, hearsay often fills the void. Before coming to China, many foreign visitors may harbor preconceived notions about the country. Travel opens doors for direct contact between different groups, which is an effective way to get rid of prejudices. "China Cool" offers countless immersive experiences that can reshape visitors' perceptions of China. When I was traveling in Germany, a friend once asked me, "Don't you find it boring to eat a bowl of plain white rice with nothing else?" I explained that in China, we don't normally eat only rice. It is accompanied by other dishes. She probably didn't know that China has such a rich variety of noodles and wheat-based foods that even a rice-loving Chinese person might struggle to name them all. Without visiting China and dining amid the crowds at a Chinese restaurant, it is difficult to understand why Chinese people eat plain white rice. You can understand only when you go there. This understanding will not come from reading a travel guide, but from sitting at a table and using chopsticks to polish off a bowl of rice and a plate of stir-fried food. Such experiences become part of memory, leaving a more lasting impression than any written account. Safety is another example. Foreigners in China might see people leaving electric scooters by the roadside with keys in the ignition, phones on restaurant tables, or belongings forgotten in shared bikes. These lost or forgotten items are returned to their owners. Such ordinary moments have a powerful effect because they are tangible and irrefutable. They can shape visitors' perceptions of safety. When foreign visitors come to China for the first time, their preconceived notions may be challenged and changed, one small moment at a time. Their connection with China unfolds everywhere: in teahouses, on bustling streets and in the ordinary moments of everyday life. Boundaries begin to fade, not because someone persuaded them, but because people share the same experiences and moments with them. The popularity of "China Cool" also reflects deeper psychological needs. Around the world, many people feel that the fast pace of modern life is draining them. There is anxiety about artificial intelligence replacing human workers, pressure from social media and fewer opportunities for meaningful face-to-face interactions. As a result, people can easily lose three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and connection with others. In today's lexicon, "cool" can mean more than just low temperature. It can mean being in control without having to make an effort, connecting with others without forcing it and being able to relax without feeling watched or judged. When a foreigner buys a cold drink on a Chinese street at 2 am and rides a shared bike through a busy crowd, the experience is no longer just traveling. It becomes: "I can live like this." At the heart of that experience is the return of a sense of control. It is the fading of psychological boundaries, and a small but meaningful reshaping of the story people tell about themselves. That may be the true essence of "China Cool". The author is an associate researcher at the Institute of Psychology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily.

item.title: Taste of the sea spikes interest, sparks innovation
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
Gently crack open a spiny sea urchin and five plump, golden lobes are revealed. Scoop one up and let it melt on your tongue. Silky and creamy, with a rich umami flavor and a hint of sweetness, it offers a taste of the sea at its late-summer best. "Top-quality sea urchins should be golden in color. They should melt in your mouth, and should not only be savory but also slightly sweet," said Yang Haiming, owner of Changxianlou Sea Urchin Restaurant in Dalian, Liaoning province. Chu shu, or End of Heat, falls on Sunday this year, marking the transition from summer to autumn. It is considered a good time to eat sea urchins in Dalian. Some farmed horse-dung sea urchins enter their peak season in August, while the locally popular "purple sea urchins" (Mesocentrotus nudus) generally pass their optimum harvesting period by late August. Located on the southern tip of the Liaodong Peninsula, Dalian borders the Yellow Sea and the Bohai Sea. Favorable water temperatures and salinity, along with abundant algae, provide suitable conditions for sea urchin growth. According to Yang, the varieties commonly found in local markets include horse-dung sea urchins and "purple sea urchins". Horse-dung urchins have shorter spines and bright orange-yellow edible lobes with a subtle sweetness. The "purple" ones have a stronger umami flavor. "One is sweeter, while the other is more savory. Both are excellent," he said. Freshness, plumpness and color are key indicators of quality. Yang said a live urchin should have actively moving spines, while its edible lobes should be plump and brightly colored when the shell is opened. Origin, weight and harvesting season should also be considered, he added. Sea urchins are also valued for their nutritional profile. The meat contains protein, unsaturated fatty acids, and vitamins and minerals, including vitamin E, iron and zinc. The nutritional composition varies by species, season, diet and habitat. Dalian locals tend to prepare sea urchins in a simple way. Fresh urchins that meet food safety standards and have been properly cleaned can be eaten directly from the shell. These can also be steamed with eggs, or served over hot rice with an egg suitable for raw consumption and seaweed flakes. Sea urchin dumplings are a Dalian specialty. Yang, who grew up by the sea and has worked as a chef for 35 years, began experimenting with urchin fillings in dumplings around 2011. Initially prepared for only friends and fellow chefs, the dumplings later became a signature dish at his restaurant. Making these dumplings requires careful handling. Once the urchins are removed from their shells, they can quickly oxidize and turn watery, so promptness is key. Each lobe also needs to be thoroughly cleaned before being turned into the filling. The urchin dumplings have since spread from Dalian to Beijing and other cities. At a newly opened Beijing branch of Xiding, a Dalian-based restaurant chain known for its urchin specialities, each dumpling weighs about 20 grams, with 12 grams of filling. Chefs use electronic scales to check the weight, boiling time is measured to the second, and the pot is covered for about 10 seconds before serving to make the dumplings rounder and plumper. "The filling contains some pork, and we use horse-dung sea urchins from Dalian," said Yu Shuangchi, head of the restaurant's kitchen. "Urchin dumplings need to be boiled slightly longer than other dumplings, mainly to bring out their umami flavor." The dough is prepared and the dumpling pockets are freshly rolled every morning, while the dumplings are assembled to order, Yu added. In Dalian, divers who harvest marine delicacies are traditionally known as hai pengzi, or sea harvesters. Some dive dozens of meters into the sea to collect deep-water sea urchins, timing their work around the tides, sometimes setting out before dawn or returning late at night. The sea urchins are then quickly brought to the kitchen, where they are served raw, steamed with eggs, or folded into dumplings — simple preparations that allow their natural flavor to shine.

item.title: Dongbi turns sunset views into thriving tourism economy
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-22
Dongbi turns sunset views into thriving village tourism economy At sunset, visitors gather along the coast of Dongbi village in Xiapu county, Ningde, Fujian province, pointing cameras toward the sea as the sky turns gold. For this traditional fishing village, the coastal scenery has become the starting point for a booming tourism economy built around photography, homestays, dining and leisure. Dongbi's tourism transformation began in August 2017 with the opening of its first homestay, Shijianhai. Its success revealed the untapped potential of tourism, prompting villagers to convert their homes while attracting outside entrepreneurs to invest. Shijianhai was later named a national Grade-A tourist homestay, the highest tier in China's national classification system. Once largely dependent on fishing and aquaculture, Dongbi has since upgraded its roads, utilities and public spaces while developing tourism-related businesses. The village now has more than 80 homestays and about 1,000 beds, according to recent local government figures. For Zheng Xianshi, a native of Dongbi, the emerging tourism industry offered a compelling reason to return home. After working outside the village in construction-site management and ride-hailing, Zheng returned and converted his family's old home into a homestay. He opened it in 2021, becoming the village's sixth homestay operator at the time. "Back then, the tourism and accommodation industry here was already doing very well," Zheng says. He later expanded his business by adding a cafe serving coffee, tea, wine and other beverages. As more businesses opened along the village's main tourist route, he says competition has increased, making distinctive experiences increasingly important. That shift is also attracting a new generation of entrepreneurs. Cai Ziyang, who previously worked in Beijing, returned to Xiapu and invested about 13 million yuan ($1.8 million) to develop Sky City, a 14-room boutique homestay that opened in 2025. Featuring an on-site restaurant, live music performances and customized travel services, the property has attracted visitors from Shanghai and across the Yangtze River Delta. For visitors, the appeal is no longer limited to photographing the sunset. They can stay in boutique homestays, experience tidal-flat activities and nearshore fishing, or spend an evening at cafes and restaurants. Sansha township, where Dongbi is located, received more than 4.6 million tourist visits in 2025, according to local reports. The township is now seeking to expand photography, cultural and creative products, marine leisure and other tourism formats. Moving forward, Dongbi plans to build on its famous sunsets by giving visitors more reasons to stay and create more opportunities for local residents to benefit from tourism, local authorities say.

item.title: Y-20 soars with national pride
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
Y-20 soars with national pride Decade-long service displays aircraft's versatility and durability The Y-20, nicknamed Kunpeng after a giant bird in Chinese mythology, is China's first domestically developed large military transport aircraft. It was officially commissioned in July 2016, marking a milestone in the strategic delivery capability of the People's Liberation Army Air Force. The project, led by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China's Xi'an Aircraft Industrial Group Co, began in 2007. Its prototype first flew in 2013 before entering service in 2016. With a maximum takeoff weight of 220 metric tons and a payload of 66 tons, Chinese pilots affectionately call it "Chubby Girl" for its wide fuselage. Ten years after its commissioning, the aircraft has not only deeply integrated itself into various combat readiness training sessions, but also displayed its power in non-military tasks such as disaster relief, humanitarian rescue and overseas transport missions. Over the decade, the aircraft itself has also evolved from a single transport platform into a family consisting of multiple variants including the original Y-20A, the Y-20B with domestically developed WS-20 engines, and the YY-20A aerial tanker. It has reached Asia, Africa, Europe and Oceania, building a channel for international exchanges and demonstrating the open, confident and pragmatic image of the Chinese military.

item.title: Ice, Chinese consumers' newest crush
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
Ice, Chinese consumers' newest crush Preference for cold drinks sparks debate on worth of traditional hot, warm beverages In China, drinking warm or hot water is a long-standing daily practice passed down through generations and believed to bring good health. However, fueled by an online buzz and changes to drinking habits, Chinese consumers — in particular social media-savvy young ones — are now putting ice, and plenty of it, in their drinks. At convenience stores, cups of ice have become a popular seller. At tea and coffee shops, "full ice, no water" has become a popular way to order a drink. Young consumers have also turned cups of ice into a social media sensation, using them to create DIY drinks that have attracted huge online attention. Gu Xiaoxiao, 36, a junior middle school teacher in Shanghai, is one of the ice drink devotees. For almost half the year, she has a cup of iced coffee at least once a day. "I usually start in April or May and keep drinking iced coffee until September or October. Besides my daily quota, I also order iced drinks when dining out or meeting friends. Recently, I even arranged to queue with friends for a popular ice cup coffee that had gone viral online," said Gu. According to a paper on China's urban consumer behavior in 2025, ice cup sales have grown by more than 300 percent for two consecutive years, with consumers in the first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangdong province's Guangzhou and Shenzhen buying an average of 48 cups per person per year, reported ThePaper.cn. Publicly available data shows that ice cups are gaining wider market penetration, expanding from plain to flavored varieties and ice cubes designed for cocktails. A search for "ice cups" on Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, returned more than 40,000 posts. Zhang Yi, CEO and chief analyst at iiMedia Research, attributed the rising demand for ice cups to the past two summers being very hot and young people wanting to make their own drinks using ice cups. "The cold chain improvement has led to a cost reduction in ice transportation. On social media, the 'full ice, no water' trend has also become a new way for people to socialize," said Zhang. "Consumers are increasingly willing to pay for ice that is cleaner and comes in more distinctive shapes," he added.

item.title: China-Africa ties: Light beyond seas, stories beyond shores
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-21
China-Africa ties: Light beyond seas, stories beyond shores Share - WeChat
At a time when narratives of civilizational divides are all too common, a forum on China-Africa media cooperation shows a different path. The 7th Forum on China-Africa Media Cooperation is underway in Beijing. Co-hosted by China's National Radio and Television Administration, the Beijing Municipal Government, and the African Union of Broadcasting, the forum brings together some 400 delegates from China and 45 African nations. It marks 70 years of China-Africa diplomatic ties and is part of the 2026 China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges.
